Codes in the predictor matrix

2026-11-16

Source: vignettes/predictor-codes.Rmd
predictor-codes.Rmd

Introduction

The predictor matrix tells mice() which variables to use when imputing a variable or block. Each row is a block to be imputed, each column a variable in the data. For the standard methods, such as pmm, norm and logreg, the entries are simple: 1 means that the column is a predictor and 0 means that it is not used (van Buuren and Groothuis-Oudshoorn 2011).

Methods for multilevel data need more information. They have to know which variable identifies the clusters, which predictors get a random effect, and whether cluster means should be added. These methods read the extra information from the same matrix, using codes such as -2, 2, 3 and 4 (van Buuren 2018, chap. 7). The codes are not the same across methods. The meaning of 2 in particular depends on the method: it is a random effect in 2l.lmer, a contextual effect in miceadds::mice.impute.2l.contextual.pmm(), and a fixed effect in jomoImpute.

This article collects the codes of the imputation methods in mice and in the packages that extend it: miceadds, micemd and mitml. It is based on the documentation and the source of mice 3.19.18, miceadds 3.20.10, micemd 1.11.0 and mitml 0.4.5.

Setting the codes

Start from the default predictor matrix and change the row of the variable to impute. In the popmis data, pupils are nested in schools. The following imputes popular with a two-level normal model, with school as cluster variable, a random slope for sex, and fixed effects for texp and teachpop:

library(mice)
#> 
#> Attaching package: 'mice'
#> The following object is masked from 'package:stats':
#> 
#>     filter
#> The following objects are masked from 'package:base':
#> 
#>     cbind, rbind
dat <- popmis[, c("school", "popular", "sex", "texp", "teachpop")]
pred <- make.predictorMatrix(dat)
pred["popular", ] <- c(-2, 0, 2, 1, 1)
pred["popular", ]
#>   school  popular      sex     texp teachpop 
#>       -2        0        2        1        1
meth <- make.method(dat)
meth["popular"] <- "2l.lmer"
imp <- mice(dat, method = meth, predictorMatrix = pred,
            m = 2, maxit = 1, seed = 1, print = FALSE)

The other variables are complete, so their rows play no role here.

Two-level methods that follow the mice convention

Most univariate two-level methods use -2 for the cluster variable, 1 for a fixed effect and 2 for a fixed plus a random effect. Some add 3 and 4 to include the cluster mean of the predictor.

Method Package -2 1 2 3 4
2l.lmer, 2l.bin mice cluster fixed fixed + random as 11 as 11
2l.norm mice cluster ignored2 fixed + random – –
2l.pan mice cluster fixed fixed + random fixed + cluster mean fixed + random + cluster mean
2l.pmm, 2l.continuous, 2l.binary miceadds cluster fixed fixed + random fixed + cluster mean fixed + random + cluster mean
2l.2stage.norm, .pmm, .bin, .pois micemd cluster fixed3 fixed + random as 13 as 13
2l.glm.norm, .bin, .pois micemd cluster fixed3 fixed + random as 13 as 13
2l.jomo micemd cluster included4 included4 – –
2lonly.mean mice cluster – – – –
2lonly.norm, 2lonly.pmm mice cluster predictor predictor – –
2lonly.function miceadds cluster5 predictor – – –

Notes:

  1. 2l.lmer and 2l.bin take all positive codes as fixed effects and 2 as a random effect. Codes 3 and 4 give no error, but they also add no cluster mean. Use 2l.pan or miceadds::mice.impute.2l.pmm() for cluster means.
  2. 2l.norm uses only -2 and 2. Predictors with code 1 are dropped without a warning. The documentation advises using 2 for all predictors.
  3. micemd documents only -2 and 2, but the source takes all positive codes as fixed effects, as in 2l.lmer.
  4. micemd::mice.impute.2l.jomo() includes all variables with a positive code in a joint random-intercept model. Code 2 does not add a random slope.
  5. miceadds recommends the argument cluster_var over code -2.

Methods that give the codes another meaning

Several methods in miceadds and micemd use the same numbers for something else. Code 2 often means that a cluster mean is added, and some methods introduce their own codes.

Method Package Codes
2l.contextual.pmm, 2l.contextual.norm miceadds -2 cluster, 1 predictor, 2 predictor + cluster mean (contextual effect)
2l.latentgroupmean.ml, 2l.latentgroupmean.mcmc miceadds -2 cluster, 1 predictor, 2 predictor + latent group mean
2l.groupmean, 2l.groupmean.elim miceadds -2 cluster, 1 or 2 variable whose cluster mean is computed
plausible.values miceadds -2 cluster, 1 predictor, 2 predictor + cluster mean, 3 item of the scale to be imputed
pls, 2l.pls2 miceadds -2 cluster (adds the cluster mean of y, leaving out the case itself), 1 predictor, 4 interactions with all other predictors, 5 quadratic term, 6 left out of the interactions
2l.2stage.heckman micemd -2 cluster, 2 predictor in the outcome and selection equations, -3 selection equation only, -4 outcome equation only (all predictors have random effects)
ml.lmer miceadds 1 fixed effect; levels and random slopes are set with the arguments levels_id, variables_levels and random_slopes, not with codes

Multivariate methods for blocks

The methods jomoImpute and panImpute impute a block of variables at once. For these methods, mice() passes the row of the block in the predictor matrix to mitml::jomoImpute() or mitml::panImpute() as its type argument, so the row contains mitml codes. These differ from the mice convention: in mitml, 2 is a fixed effect and 3 a random effect.

Code Meaning in mitml::jomoImpute() and mitml::panImpute()
1 target variable with missing data
2 predictor with a fixed effect on all targets (complete)
3 predictor with a random effect on all targets (complete)
-1 grouping variable; the model is fitted separately within each group
-2 cluster indicator
0 not in the model

panImpute requires a cluster indicator (-2) and at least one random effect. The default predictor matrix gives every variable code 1, so complete variables also enter the model as targets. Set them to 2 or 3 to use them as predictors instead.

The following imputes bmi, chl and hyp jointly with jomoImpute, with age as a fixed-effect predictor:

blocks <- make.blocks(list(B1 = c("bmi", "chl", "hyp"), age = "age"))
pred <- make.predictorMatrix(nhanes, blocks)
pred["B1", "age"] <- 2
pred
#>     age bmi hyp chl
#> B1    2   1   1   1
#> age   0   1   1   1
imp <- mice(nhanes, blocks = blocks, method = c("jomoImpute", ""),
            predictorMatrix = pred, maxit = 1, seed = 1, print = FALSE)

The variables in the block are always passed as targets (1), unless the row sets another code for them, such as -2 for a cluster indicator. This matters for an unnamed block with a single variable, which is named after its variable. make.predictorMatrix() sets that variable to 0 in its own row. Before mice 3.19.18, jomoImpute therefore left the variable out of the model and stopped with “Target variables do not contain any missing data” (#379).

Checking the codes

mice() does not check whether the codes fit the method. A code that the method does not know is usually ignored or treated as another code, without a warning. To see what was used, inspect the predictor matrix and the methods stored in the result:

imp$predictorMatrix
#>     age bmi hyp chl
#> B1    2   1   1   1
#> age   0   1   1   1
imp$method
#>           B1          age 
#> "jomoImpute"           ""

When in doubt, check the help page of the method, for example ?mice.impute.2l.pan or ?miceadds::mice.impute.2l.contextual.pmm.

References

van Buuren, S., and K. Groothuis-Oudshoorn. 2011. “mice: Multivariate Imputation by Chained Equations in R.” Journal of Statistical Software 45 (3): 1–67. https://doi.org/10.18637/jss.v045.i03.
van Buuren, Stef. 2018. Flexible Imputation of Missing Data. 2nd ed. Interdisciplinary Statistics Series. Chapman and Hall/CRC. https://doi.org/10.1201/9780429492259.
